front: A single node \(V\) connects to a \(12\ \text{V}\) source through a \(4\ \Omega\) resistor, to a \(6\ \text{V}\) source through a \(12\ \Omega\) resistor, and to ground through a \(6\ \Omega\) resistor (both source references grounded). Find the node voltage \(V\).
explanation: Apply KCL at the node: \(\dfrac{V-12}{4} + \dfrac{V-6}{12} + \dfrac{V}{6} = 0\). Multiply by \(12\): \(3(V-12) + (V-6) + 2V = 0\), giving \(6V = 42\), so \(V = 7\ \text{V}\).

front: Three \(9\ \Omega\) resistors are connected in a balanced delta (\(\Delta\)). Find the resistance of each branch of the equivalent wye (Y) network.
explanation: For a balanced delta, each wye resistor is \(R_Y = \dfrac{R_\Delta\, R_\Delta}{R_\Delta + R_\Delta + R_\Delta} = \dfrac{R_\Delta}{3}\). Thus \(R_Y = \dfrac{9}{3} = 3\ \Omega\).

front: Convert a \(6\ \text{A}\) current source in parallel with a \(10\ \Omega\) resistor into its equivalent Thevenin (voltage-source) form.
explanation: A source transformation keeps the resistance and sets \(V_s = I_s R = (6\ \text{A})(10\ \Omega) = 60\ \text{V}\). The equivalent is a \(60\ \text{V}\) source in series with \(10\ \Omega\).

front: A \(100\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is charged to \(200\ \text{V}\). How much energy is stored in it?
An inductor \(L = 50\ \text{mH}\) carries a steady DC current of \(4\ \text{A}\). Find the energy stored in its magnetic field.
A series RL circuit with \(R = 25\ \Omega\) and \(L = 50\ \text{mH}\) is connected to a \(100\ \text{V}\) DC source at \(t = 0\) with zero initial current. Find the current at \(t = 2\ \text{ms}\).
explanation: Time constant \(\tau = L/R = 0.05/25 = 2\ \text{ms}\); final current \(i(\infty) = V/R = 100/25 = 4\ \text{A}\). At \(t = \tau\): \(i = 4(1 - e^{-1}) = 4(0.632) \approx 2.53\ \text{A}\).

front: A series RC circuit has \(R = 40\ \Omega\) and capacitive reactance \(X_C = 30\ \Omega\), driven by \(V = 120\angle{0^{\circ}}\ \text{V}\) (rms). Find the phasor current.
explanation: Impedance: \(Z = 40 - j30 = 50\angle{-36.9^{\circ}}\ \Omega\). Then \(I = \dfrac{V}{Z} = \dfrac{120\angle{0^{\circ}}}{50\angle{-36.9^{\circ}}} = 2.4\angle{36.9^{\circ}}\ \text{A}\) (current leads the voltage).

front: A series RLC circuit has \(R = 6\ \Omega\), \(L = 9\ \text{mH}\), and \(C = 10\ \mu\text{F}\). Find the quality factor \(Q\) and the bandwidth (in rad/s).
explanation: Resonance: \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC} = 1/\sqrt{(9\times10^{-3})(10\times10^{-6})} \approx 3333\ \text{rad/s}\). Quality factor: \(Q = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}} = \dfrac{1}{6}\sqrt{900} = 5\). Bandwidth: \(\text{BW} = \omega_0/Q \approx 667\ \text{rad/s}\).

front: A single-phase load absorbs \(P = 1.2\ \text{kW}\) at a power factor of \(0.6\) lagging. Find the apparent power \(S\) and the reactive power \(Q\).
explanation: Apparent power: \(S = P/\text{pf} = 1200/0.6 = 2000\ \text{VA}\). With \(\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.6) = 53.1^{\circ}\), \(Q = S\sin\theta = 2000(0.8) = 1600\ \text{VAR}\) (equivalently \(Q = \sqrt{S^{2}-P^{2}}\)).

front: Find the rms value of the periodic voltage \(v(t) = 6 + 8\cos(\omega t)\ \text{V}\).
explanation: A DC term and a sinusoid combine in quadrature: \(V_{rms} = \sqrt{V_{DC}^{2} + \left(\dfrac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{6^{2} + \dfrac{8^{2}}{2}} = \sqrt{36 + 32} = \sqrt{68} \approx 8.25\ \text{V}\).

front: A resistor \(R = 50\ \Omega\) has the voltage \(v(t) = 100\cos(377t)\ \text{V}\) across it. Find the average power dissipated.
explanation: The rms voltage is \(V_{rms} = 100/\sqrt{2}\ \text{V}\). Average power in a resistor: \(P = \dfrac{V_{rms}^{2}}{R} = \dfrac{(100/\sqrt{2})^{2}}{50} = \dfrac{5000}{50} = 100\ \text{W}\).

front: Express \(v(t) = 3\cos(\omega t) + 4\sin(\omega t)\ \text{V}\) as a single sinusoid of the form \(V_m\cos(\omega t + \phi)\).
explanation: Using a cosine reference, \(4\sin(\omega t) = 4\cos(\omega t - 90^{\circ})\), so the phasor sum is \(3\angle{0^{\circ}} + 4\angle{-90^{\circ}} = 3 - j4 = 5\angle{-53.1^{\circ}}\). Hence \(v(t) = 5\cos(\omega t - 53.1^{\circ})\ \text{V}\).

front: At \(\omega = 1000\ \text{rad/s}\), a \(50\ \Omega\) resistor is in parallel with a \(0.1\ \text{H}\) inductor. Find the equivalent impedance in rectangular form.
explanation: Inductor impedance: \(Z_L = j\omega L = j(1000)(0.1) = j100\ \Omega\). Parallel combination: \(Z = \dfrac{(50)(j100)}{50 + j100} = \dfrac{j5000}{50 + j100} = 40 + j20\ \Omega\).

front: A \(20\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor charges through a \(100\ \text{k}\Omega\) resistor from a \(50\ \text{V}\) source (initially uncharged). How long until the capacitor voltage reaches \(30\ \text{V}\)?
explanation: Time constant \(\tau = RC = (100\times10^{3})(20\times10^{-6}) = 2\ \text{s}\). From \(v = V(1 - e^{-t/\tau})\): \(30 = 50(1 - e^{-t/2})\Rightarrow e^{-t/2} = 0.4\Rightarrow t = 2\ln(2.5) \approx 1.83\ \text{s}\).

front: In DC steady state, a \(12\ \text{V}\) source drives a \(3\ \Omega\) resistor in series with a \(6\ \Omega\) resistor to ground, and a capacitor is connected across the \(6\ \Omega\) resistor. Find the steady-state capacitor voltage.
explanation: In DC steady state a capacitor draws no current (it acts as an open circuit), so the series current flows only through the two resistors. The capacitor voltage equals the \(6\ \Omega\) voltage: \(V_C = 12\cdot\dfrac{6}{3+6} = 8\ \text{V}\).

front: An amplitude-modulated (AM) waveform has an envelope that varies between a maximum of \(V_{\max}=12\ \text{V}\) and a minimum of \(V_{\min}=4\ \text{V}\). Determine the modulation index \(m\).
explanation: For AM the envelope peaks are \(V_{\max}=A_c(1+m)\) and \(V_{\min}=A_c(1-m)\). Solving for \(m\): \[m=\frac{V_{\max}-V_{\min}}{V_{\max}+V_{\min}}=\frac{12-4}{12+4}=\frac{8}{16}=0.5.\] The carrier is 50% modulated.

front: An AM transmitter radiates a carrier power of \(P_c=500\ \text{W}\) and is modulated by a single tone to a depth of \(m=0.6\). Find the total power contained in the two sidebands.
explanation: Total transmitted power is \(P_t=P_c\left(1+\tfrac{m^2}{2}\right)\), so the sideband power is the excess over the carrier: \[P_{sb}=P_c\cdot\frac{m^2}{2}=500\cdot\frac{0.6^2}{2}=500\cdot0.18=90\ \text{W}.\] The upper and lower sidebands share this equally, 45 W each.

front: A frequency-modulated (FM) signal has a peak frequency deviation of \(\Delta f=75\ \text{kHz}\) when the modulating tone frequency is \(f_m=15\ \text{kHz}\). Determine the modulation index \(\beta\).
explanation: The FM modulation index is the ratio of peak frequency deviation to modulating frequency: \[\beta=\frac{\Delta f}{f_m}=\frac{75\ \text{kHz}}{15\ \text{kHz}}=5.\]

front: An FM signal has a peak frequency deviation of \(\Delta f=30\ \text{kHz}\) and a highest modulating frequency of \(f_m=5\ \text{kHz}\). Estimate the transmission bandwidth using Carson's rule.
explanation: Carson's rule estimates the FM bandwidth as \[B=2(\Delta f+f_m)=2(30\ \text{kHz}+5\ \text{kHz})=2(35\ \text{kHz})=70\ \text{kHz}.\]

front: An angle-modulated signal is \(v(t)=10\cos\!\left[2\pi(10^{8})t+6\sin\!\left(2\pi(10^{3})t\right)\right]\ \text{V}\). Treating it as an FM signal, find the peak frequency deviation \(\Delta f\).
explanation: The phase term is \(\beta\sin(2\pi f_m t)\) with modulation index \(\beta=6\) and modulating frequency \(f_m=10^{3}\ \text{Hz}\). For FM \(\beta=\Delta f/f_m\), so \[\Delta f=\beta f_m=6\times1000\ \text{Hz}=6\ \text{kHz}.\]

front: An analog voice signal band-limited to \(4\ \text{kHz}\) is sampled at the Nyquist rate, and each sample is encoded with \(8\) bits. Determine the PCM bit rate.
explanation: The Nyquist sampling rate is \(f_s=2\times4\ \text{kHz}=8000\ \text{samples/s}\). With \(8\) bits per sample, \[R=f_s\times n=8000\times8=64{,}000\ \text{bps}=64\ \text{kbps}.\]

front: A PCM system uses \(L=64\) uniform quantization levels. How many bits are required to encode each sample?
explanation: The number of bits \(n\) must satisfy \(2^{n}\ge L\). For \(L=64\): \[n=\log_2 64=6\ \text{bits}\quad(2^6=64).\]

front: For a uniform \(n\)-bit PCM quantizer, the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio is approximately \(\text{SNR}\approx(6.02n+1.76)\ \text{dB}\). Estimate the SNR of a \(10\)-bit quantizer.
explanation: Substitute \(n=10\): \[\text{SNR}\approx6.02(10)+1.76=60.2+1.76=61.96\approx62\ \text{dB}.\]

front: An amplifier raises a signal's power from \(2\ \text{mW}\) to \(200\ \text{mW}\). Express the power gain in decibels.
A receiver detects an input signal power of \(1\ \mu\text{W}\). Express this power level in dBm.
explanation: dBm references power to 1 mW: \[P_{\text{dBm}}=10\log_{10}\!\frac{P}{1\ \text{mW}}=10\log_{10}\!\frac{10^{-6}\ \text{W}}{10^{-3}\ \text{W}}=10\log_{10}(10^{-3})=-30\ \text{dBm}.\]

front: A communication receiver has a signal power of \(50\ \text{mW}\) and a noise power of \(50\ \mu\text{W}\). Express the signal-to-noise ratio in decibels.
explanation: First form the linear ratio: \(\text{SNR}=\dfrac{50\ \text{mW}}{0.05\ \text{mW}}=1000\). Then \[\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}}=10\log_{10}(1000)=10(3)=30\ \text{dB}.\]

front: A modem transmits at a symbol (baud) rate of \(2400\ \text{symbols/s}\) using \(16\)-QAM. Determine the resulting bit rate.
explanation: Each \(16\)-QAM symbol carries \(\log_2 16=4\) bits. Therefore \[R_b=R_s\times\log_2 M=2400\times4=9600\ \text{bps}.\]

front: A QPSK link carries a bit rate of \(2\ \text{Mbps}\). Determine the channel symbol (baud) rate.
explanation: QPSK maps \(\log_2 4=2\) bits onto each symbol, so the symbol rate is \[R_s=\frac{R_b}{\log_2 M}=\frac{2\times10^{6}}{2}=1\times10^{6}\ \text{symbols/s}=1\ \text{Mbaud}.\]

front: A noiseless channel of bandwidth \(B=3\ \text{kHz}\) transmits using \(M=4\) discrete signal levels. Using the Nyquist relation, find the maximum data rate.
explanation: The Nyquist capacity of a noiseless channel is \[C=2B\log_2 M=2(3000)\log_2 4=2(3000)(2)=12{,}000\ \text{bps}=12\ \text{kbps}.\]

front: A channel has a bandwidth of \(B=3\ \text{kHz}\) and a signal-to-noise power ratio of \(7\). Find the Shannon channel capacity.
explanation: The Shannon-Hartley capacity is \[C=B\log_2(1+\text{SNR})=3000\log_2(1+7)=3000\log_2 8=3000(3)=9000\ \text{bps}=9\ \text{kbps}.\]

front: A discrete source emits one of \(8\) equally likely symbols. How much information (in bits) does each symbol convey?
explanation: For an equally likely symbol with probability \(p=1/8\), the self-information is \[I=\log_2\frac{1}{p}=\log_2 8=3\ \text{bits}.\]

front: A source emits four symbols with probabilities \(\{\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac18,\tfrac18\}\). Compute the source entropy \(H\).
explanation: Entropy is \(H=\sum p_i\log_2(1/p_i)\): \[H=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac18(3)+\tfrac18(3)=0.5+0.5+0.375+0.375=1.75\ \text{bits/symbol}.\]

front: A \((7,4)\) Hamming code maps \(4\) data bits into a \(7\)-bit codeword. Determine the code rate.
explanation: Code rate is the ratio of information bits to total transmitted bits: \[R=\frac{k}{n}=\frac{4}{7}\approx0.571.\] The remaining \(3\) bits are parity checks.

front: A subnet uses the CIDR prefix \(/26\). How many usable host addresses are available per subnet?
explanation: Host bits: \(32 - 26 = 6\). Total addresses per subnet: \(2^{6} = 64\). Exclude the network and broadcast addresses: \(64 - 2 = 62\) usable hosts.

front: A Class C network \(192.168.10.0/24\) is subnetted with a \(/28\) mask. How many subnets are created, and how many usable hosts does each subnet support?
explanation: Borrowed bits: \(28 - 24 = 4 \Rightarrow 2^{4} = 16\) subnets. Host bits: \(32 - 28 = 4 \Rightarrow 2^{4} - 2 = 14\) usable hosts per subnet.

front: A host is configured with IP address \(192.168.1.200\) and subnet mask \(255.255.255.192\) (\(/26\)). What is its network (subnet) address?
explanation: For \(/26\), the block size in the last octet is \(256 - 192 = 64\). Subnet boundaries are \(0, 64, 128, 192\). Since \(192 \le 200 \le 255\), the host lies in the block starting at \(192\), so the network address is \(192.168.1.192\).

front: A subnet has network address \(172.16.20.0\) with mask \(255.255.255.224\) (\(/27\)). What is the subnet's broadcast address?
explanation: For \(/27\), host bits \(= 5\) and block size \(= 2^{5} = 32\). The subnet spans \(172.16.20.0\) through \(172.16.20.31\). The broadcast address is the last address in the block: \(172.16.20.31\).

front: A single subnet must accommodate at least \(500\) hosts. What is the smallest subnet (longest prefix) in CIDR notation that satisfies this requirement?
Express the subnet mask \(255.255.255.240\) in CIDR (slash) prefix notation.
explanation: Each \(255\) octet contributes \(8\) one-bits: \(3 \times 8 = 24\). The last octet \(240 = 11110000_{2}\) contributes \(4\) one-bits. Total \(= 24 + 4 = 28\), so the mask is \(/28\).

front: A \(1500\)-byte packet is sent over a link of bandwidth \(10\ \text{Mbps}\). Neglecting propagation delay, find the transmission (serialization) delay.
explanation: Packet size in bits: \(1500 \times 8 = 12{,}000\ \text{bits}\). Transmission delay \(= \dfrac{\text{bits}}{\text{rate}} = \dfrac{12{,}000}{10 \times 10^{6}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s} = 1.2\ \text{ms}\).

front: A signal propagates at \(2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}\) along a \(300\ \text{km}\) link. Find the propagation delay.
explanation: Propagation delay \(= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \dfrac{300 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m}}{2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s} = 1.5\ \text{ms}\).

front: A link has bandwidth \(1\ \text{Mbps}\) and one-way propagation delay \(20\ \text{ms}\). Compute the bandwidth-delay product in bits.
explanation: Bandwidth-delay product \(= \text{bandwidth} \times \text{delay} = (1 \times 10^{6}\ \text{bits/s}) \times (20 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}) = 20{,}000\ \text{bits}\). This equals the number of bits in flight filling the link.

front: A \(5\ \text{MB}\) file (use \(1\ \text{MB} = 10^{6}\ \text{bytes}\)) is sent over a \(100\ \text{Mbps}\) link with one-way propagation delay \(10\ \text{ms}\). Find the total time for the last bit to arrive.
explanation: Bits: \(5 \times 10^{6} \times 8 = 4 \times 10^{7}\ \text{bits}\). Transmission time \(= \dfrac{4 \times 10^{7}}{100 \times 10^{6}} = 0.4\ \text{s}\). Total \(= 0.4 + 0.01 = 0.41\ \text{s}\).

front: A TCP connection has a maximum receive window of \(64\ \text{KiB}\) (\(65{,}536\) bytes) over a path with \(\text{RTT} = 40\ \text{ms}\). Estimate the maximum achievable throughput.
explanation: Throughput \(\approx \dfrac{\text{window}}{\text{RTT}} = \dfrac{65{,}536 \times 8\ \text{bits}}{40 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}} = \dfrac{524{,}288}{0.04} \approx 1.31 \times 10^{7}\ \text{bps} \approx 13.1\ \text{Mbps}\).

front: In a stop-and-wait ARQ link the frame transmission time is \(1\ \text{ms}\) and the one-way propagation delay is \(4\ \text{ms}\). Neglecting ACK and processing time, find the link utilization.
explanation: Utilization \(U = \dfrac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p} = \dfrac{1}{1 + 2(4)} = \dfrac{1}{9} \approx 0.111 = 11.1\%\).

front: A \(10\ \text{Mbps}\) link has \(\text{RTT} = 30\ \text{ms}\) and uses \(1250\)-byte frames. What minimum sliding-window size (in frames) is needed to fully utilize the link?
explanation: Frame transmission time \(T_t = \dfrac{1250 \times 8}{10 \times 10^{6}} = 1\ \text{ms}\). Full utilization needs \(W \ge 1 + \dfrac{\text{RTT}}{T_t} = 1 + \dfrac{30}{1} = 31\) frames.

front: A Go-Back-N protocol uses a sender window size of \(15\). What is the minimum number of bits required for the sequence-number field?
explanation: Go-Back-N requires the sequence-number space to satisfy \(2^{m} \ge W + 1\). With \(W = 15\): \(2^{m} \ge 16\), so \(m = 4\) bits (\(2^{4} = 16\)).

front: A noiseless channel has bandwidth \(3\ \text{kHz}\) and uses \(4\) signal levels. Using Nyquist's theorem, find the maximum data rate.
A channel has bandwidth \(4\ \text{kHz}\) and signal-to-noise ratio \(\text{SNR} = 1023\) (linear). Using the Shannon-Hartley theorem, find the channel capacity.
A telephone channel has bandwidth \(3.4\ \text{kHz}\) and \(\text{SNR} = 30\ \text{dB}\). Estimate the Shannon channel capacity.
explanation: Convert dB to linear: \(\text{SNR} = 10^{30/10} = 1000\). Then \(C = B\log_{2}(1 + \text{SNR}) = 3400\log_{2}(1001) \approx 3400 \times 9.97 \approx 33{,}900\ \text{bps} \approx 33.9\ \text{kbps}\).

front: A \(10\ \text{Mbps}\) link uses Manchester line encoding. What is the required signaling (baud) rate?
explanation: Manchester encoding places a transition in the middle of every bit, giving up to \(2\) signal elements per bit. Signal rate \(= 2 \times\) data rate \(= 2 \times 10\ \text{Mbps} = 20\ \text{Mbaud}\).

front: An IPv4 packet carries a TCP segment with a \(20\)-byte IPv4 header, a \(20\)-byte TCP header, and \(1460\) bytes of application data. What is the protocol efficiency (payload divided by total bytes)?
explanation: Total size \(= 20 + 20 + 1460 = 1500\ \text{bytes}\) (the typical Ethernet MTU). Efficiency \(= \dfrac{1460}{1500} \approx 0.973 = 97.3\%\).

front: In the TCP/IP model, the transport layer passes a segment down to the network layer. What is the resulting network-layer protocol data unit (PDU) called, and what does the network layer add to form it?
back: A packet (IP datagram); the network layer prepends an IP header containing source and destination IP addresses
explanation: Encapsulation adds a header at each layer. The transport-layer PDU is a segment; the network layer wraps it with an IP header (source/destination IP addresses, TTL, protocol, etc.) to form a packet (datagram); the data-link layer then adds its own header and trailer to form a frame.

front: An 8-bit register holds the two's-complement bit pattern \(11010011_2\). What signed decimal integer does it represent?
explanation: The MSB is 1, so the value is negative. Find its magnitude by taking the two's complement: invert \(11010011\to00101100\) and add 1 to get \(00101101=45\). Hence the stored value is \(-45\). Check by weighted sum: \(-128+64+16+2+1=-45\).

front: Represent the decimal integer \(-37\) in 8-bit two's-complement form.
Two 8-bit signed (two's-complement) numbers \(01011010\) and \(00110000\) are added. Give the 8-bit sum and state whether signed overflow occurs.
explanation: In decimal the operands are \(+90\) and \(+48\). Binary addition gives \(01011010+00110000=10001010\), which as two's complement is \(-118\). But \(90+48=138\) exceeds the 8-bit signed maximum \(+127\); two positive operands yielding a negative result signals overflow.

front: What is the range of integers representable in a 12-bit two's-complement format?
A byte-addressable memory has a capacity of \(64\ \text{KiB}\). How many address lines are required to uniquely access every byte?
explanation: \(64\ \text{KiB}=64\times1024=2^{16}\) bytes. The number of address lines needed is \(\log_2(2^{16})=16\).

front: A processor has a 24-bit address bus and is byte-addressable. What is the maximum amount of memory it can directly address?
explanation: Each address selects one byte, and a 24-bit bus provides \(2^{24}\) distinct addresses. \(2^{24}=16{,}777{,}216\) bytes \(=16\ \text{MiB}\).

front: How many \(8\text{K}\times 8\) memory chips are needed to construct a \(64\text{K}\times 16\) memory system?
explanation: Depth: \(64\text{K}/8\text{K}=8\) chips stacked to reach 64K locations. Width: \(16/8=2\) chips to form each 16-bit word. Total \(=8\times2=16\) chips.

front: A cache has a hit time of \(2\ \text{ns}\) and a miss penalty of \(80\ \text{ns}\). If the miss rate is \(4\%\), find the average memory access time (AMAT).
explanation: \(\text{AMAT}=\text{hit time}+\text{miss rate}\times\text{miss penalty}=2+0.04\times80=2+3.2=5.2\ \text{ns}\).

front: A byte-addressable system uses a direct-mapped cache with \(16\ \text{KiB}\) of data and a \(32\)-byte block (line) size. Find (a) the number of cache lines and (b) the number of index bits.
explanation: Number of lines \(=\dfrac{16\ \text{KiB}}{32\ \text{B}}=\dfrac{16384}{32}=512\). The index selects one of these lines, so index bits \(=\log_2(512)=9\).

front: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has a clock period of \(2\ \text{ns}\). Assuming no stalls, how long does it take to execute \(50\) instructions?
explanation: A \(k\)-stage pipeline completes \(n\) instructions in \(k+n-1\) cycles: \(5+50-1=54\) cycles. Time \(=54\times2\ \text{ns}=108\ \text{ns}\).

front: A program of \(1000\) instructions runs on an ideal 5-stage pipeline (one cycle per stage, no stalls). Compared with a non-pipelined design that takes 5 cycles per instruction, what is the speedup?
explanation: Non-pipelined time \(=1000\times5=5000\) cycles. Pipelined time \(=k+n-1=5+1000-1=1004\) cycles. Speedup \(=\dfrac{5000}{1004}\approx4.98\).

front: A program executes \(5\times10^{6}\) instructions with an average CPI of \(3\) on a \(1\ \text{GHz}\) processor. Find the CPU execution time.
explanation: Total clock cycles \(=5\times10^{6}\times3=1.5\times10^{7}\). Execution time \(=\dfrac{\text{cycles}}{\text{clock rate}}=\dfrac{1.5\times10^{7}}{1\times10^{9}}=0.015\ \text{s}=15\ \text{ms}\).

front: A processor is clocked at \(2\ \text{GHz}\) and executes a program with an average CPI of \(2.5\). Determine its MIPS rating.
explanation: \(\text{MIPS}=\dfrac{\text{clock rate}}{\text{CPI}\times10^{6}}=\dfrac{2\times10^{9}}{2.5\times10^{6}}=800\).

front: A program's dynamic instruction mix is \(40\%\) loads (CPI 2), \(20\%\) stores (CPI 2), \(30\%\) ALU operations (CPI 1), and \(10\%\) branches (CPI 3). Find the average CPI.
A program spends \(60\%\) of its execution time in a routine that is then sped up by a factor of \(3\). By Amdahl's law, what is the overall speedup?
explanation: Amdahl's law: \(\text{speedup}=\dfrac{1}{(1-f)+f/s}\) with \(f=0.6\), \(s=3\). \(\text{speedup}=\dfrac{1}{0.4+0.6/3}=\dfrac{1}{0.4+0.2}=\dfrac{1}{0.6}\approx1.67\).

front: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs to locate a key in a sorted array of \(1000\) elements?
explanation: Binary search halves the search interval each step, requiring \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) comparisons in the worst case. Since \(2^{9}=512<1000\le1024=2^{10}\), the maximum is \(10\).

front: A binary tree has 6 levels (root at level 0, deepest leaves at level 5). What is the maximum number of nodes it can contain?
explanation: A full binary tree holds \(2^{i}\) nodes at level \(i\). Summing all levels: \(2^{0}+2^{1}+\cdots+2^{5}=2^{6}-1=63\).

front: A synchronous data bus is \(32\) bits wide and runs at \(200\ \text{MHz}\), transferring one word per clock cycle. What is its maximum data-transfer rate in bytes per second?
explanation: Each transfer moves \(32\ \text{bits}=4\ \text{bytes}\). At \(200\times10^{6}\) transfers per second: \(4\times200\times10^{6}=8\times10^{8}=800\ \text{MB/s}\).

front: Using 8-bit two's-complement arithmetic, compute \(35-18\) by adding \(35\) to the two's complement of \(18\). Give the 8-bit result and its decimal value.
Find the transfer function \(T(s)=Y(s)/U(s)\) and its poles for the system \(\ddot{y}+7\dot{y}+12y=3u(t)\) with zero initial conditions.
explanation: 1) Laplace transform with zero initial conditions: \((s^{2}+7s+12)Y(s)=3U(s)\). 2) Divide: \(T(s)=\dfrac{3}{s^{2}+7s+12}\). 3) Factor the denominator: \(s^{2}+7s+12=(s+3)(s+4)\), so the poles are \(s=-3\) and \(s=-4\).

front: A second-order system has characteristic equation \(s^{2}+4s+25=0\). Find the natural frequency \(\omega_n\), the damping ratio \(\zeta\), and classify the response.
explanation: 1) Compare with \(s^{2}+2\zeta\omega_n s+\omega_n^{2}\). 2) \(\omega_n^{2}=25\Rightarrow\omega_n=5\ \text{rad/s}\). 3) \(2\zeta\omega_n=4\Rightarrow\zeta=\dfrac{4}{2(5)}=0.4\). 4) Since \(0<\zeta<1\), the response is underdamped.

front: A second-order system has damping ratio \(\zeta=0.6\). Estimate the percent overshoot of its unit-step response.
Classify the transient response and stability of a system with characteristic equation \(s^{2}+7s+10=0\).
back: Overdamped and stable (real, distinct poles \(s=-2\) and \(s=-5\)).
explanation: 1) Factor: \(s^{2}+7s+10=(s+2)(s+5)\). 2) Poles are \(s=-2\) and \(s=-5\). 3) Both are real, distinct, and negative, so the system is stable and the response is overdamped.

front: Use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to determine the number of right-half-plane roots of \(s^{4}+2s^{3}+3s^{2}+4s+5=0\).
back: Two right-half-plane roots; the system is unstable.

front: A unity-feedback system has open-loop transfer function \(G(s)=\dfrac{K}{s(s+2)(s+6)}\). Find the range of \(K>0\) for closed-loop stability.
For a unity-feedback system with \(G(s)=\dfrac{40}{(s+2)(s+4)}\), find the steady-state error to a unit-step input.
explanation: 1) This is a type-0 system; use the position error constant \(K_p=\lim_{s\to0}G(s)=\dfrac{40}{(2)(4)}=5\). 2) For a unit step, \(e_{ss}=\dfrac{1}{1+K_p}\). 3) \(e_{ss}=\dfrac{1}{1+5}=\dfrac{1}{6}\approx0.167\).

front: For a unity-feedback system with \(G(s)=\dfrac{80}{s(s+4)}\), find the steady-state error to a unit-ramp input.
explanation: 1) This is a type-1 system; use the velocity error constant \(K_v=\lim_{s\to0}sG(s)=\dfrac{80}{4}=20\). 2) For a unit ramp, \(e_{ss}=\dfrac{1}{K_v}\). 3) \(e_{ss}=\dfrac{1}{20}=0.05\).

front: A unity-feedback type-0 system has \(G(s)=\dfrac{30}{(s+3)(s+5)}\). Find the steady-state error to a unit-ramp input.
explanation: 1) The velocity error constant is \(K_v=\lim_{s\to0}sG(s)\). 2) With no pole at the origin, \(K_v=0\cdot\dfrac{30}{(3)(5)}=0\). 3) For a ramp, \(e_{ss}=\dfrac{1}{K_v}=\infty\); a type-0 system cannot follow a ramp input.

front: A first-order system has transfer function \(G(s)=\dfrac{8}{s+4}\). Find its time constant \(\tau\) and its 2% settling time.
explanation: 1) The pole is at \(s=-4\), so \(\tau=\dfrac{1}{4}=0.25\ \text{s}\). 2) For a first-order system the 2% settling time is \(T_s\approx4\tau\). 3) \(T_s\approx4(0.25)=1\ \text{s}\).

front: For the second-order system \(T(s)=\dfrac{25}{s^{2}+2s+25}\), estimate the 2% settling time and the damped natural frequency.
explanation: 1) \(\omega_n=\sqrt{25}=5\ \text{rad/s}\); \(2\zeta\omega_n=2\Rightarrow\zeta=0.2\). 2) \(T_s\approx\dfrac{4}{\zeta\omega_n}=\dfrac{4}{1}=4\ \text{s}\). 3) \(\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^{2}}=5\sqrt{0.96}\approx4.9\ \text{rad/s}\).

front: A system has forward-path transfer function \(G(s)=\dfrac{20}{s+3}\) and a negative-feedback path \(H(s)=0.25\). Find the closed-loop transfer function.
A unity-feedback system has forward-path transfer function \(G(s)=\dfrac{2}{s(s+3)}\). Find the closed-loop transfer function and its poles.
explanation: 1) For unity feedback, \(T(s)=\dfrac{G}{1+G}=\dfrac{2}{s(s+3)+2}\). 2) Expand: \(s(s+3)+2=s^{2}+3s+2\). 3) Factor \((s+1)(s+2)\), so the closed-loop poles are \(s=-1\) and \(s=-2\).

front: For \(G(s)=\dfrac{20}{s+5}\), state the break (corner) frequency of its Bode plot and the DC gain in decibels.
explanation: 1) The pole at \(s=-5\) sets the corner frequency \(\omega=5\ \text{rad/s}\). 2) The DC gain is \(G(0)=\dfrac{20}{5}=4\). 3) In decibels, \(20\log_{10}(4)\approx12\ \text{dB}\).

front: Convert the binary number \(10110110_2\) to hexadecimal.
Convert the decimal fraction \(0.625_{10}\) to binary.
explanation: Repeatedly multiply the fractional part by 2 and record each integer part: \(0.625\times 2 = 1.25\) (1), \(0.25\times 2 = 0.5\) (0), \(0.5\times 2 = 1.0\) (1). Reading the recorded bits top-to-bottom gives \(0.101_2\). Check: \(2^{-1} + 2^{-3} = 0.5 + 0.125 = 0.625\).

front: Represent the decimal number \(47\) in 8-4-2-1 BCD (binary-coded decimal).
explanation: In BCD each decimal digit is encoded separately using 4 bits. The digit \(4 = 0100\) and the digit \(7 = 0111\), so \(47_{10} = 0100\;0111\) in BCD.

front: Convert the binary number \(1011_2\) to its Gray code equivalent.
explanation: The MSB of the Gray code equals the MSB of the binary value; each lower Gray bit is the XOR of adjacent binary bits. \(G_3 = B_3 = 1\); \(G_2 = B_3\oplus B_2 = 1\oplus 0 = 1\); \(G_1 = B_2\oplus B_1 = 0\oplus 1 = 1\); \(G_0 = B_1\oplus B_0 = 1\oplus 1 = 0\). The Gray code is \(1110\).

front: Find the 8-bit two's-complement representation of \(-53\).
The 8-bit two's-complement value \(B9_{16}\) is held in a register. What signed decimal number does it represent?
explanation: \(B9_{16} = 10111001_2\). The MSB is 1, so the value is negative. Take the two's complement of the magnitude: invert to \(01000110\) and add 1 to obtain \(01000111 = 71\). Hence the value is \(-71\). Check: \(-128 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 1 = -71\).

front: Using 6-bit two's-complement arithmetic, compute \(13 - 6\) and give the binary result.
explanation: Represent \(+13 = 001101\). Form \(-6\): \(6 = 000110\), invert to \(111001\), add 1 to get \(111010\). Add the two: \(001101 + 111010 = 1\,000111\). Discard the carry out of the 6th bit, leaving \(000111_2 = 7 = 13 - 6\).

front: Simplify the Boolean expression \(F = A + \bar{A}B\).
explanation: By the redundancy (absorption) law, \(A + \bar{A}B = (A + \bar{A})(A + B) = 1\cdot(A + B) = A + B\). Intuitively, when \(A = 1\) the output is already 1, and when \(A = 0\) the term \(\bar{A}B\) reduces to \(B\).

front: Simplify \(F = AB + \bar{A}C + BC\) using the consensus theorem.
explanation: The consensus term of \(AB\) and \(\bar{A}C\) (formed by removing the variable \(A\), which appears uncomplemented in one term and complemented in the other) is \(BC\). The consensus theorem states this term is redundant, so it can be dropped: \(F = AB + \bar{A}C\).

front: Use DeMorgan's theorem to write the complement of \(F = AB + CD\) as a product of sums.
explanation: \(\bar{F} = \overline{AB + CD} = \overline{AB}\cdot\overline{CD}\). Applying DeMorgan's theorem to each factor gives \(\overline{AB} = \bar{A} + \bar{B}\) and \(\overline{CD} = \bar{C} + \bar{D}\). Therefore \(\bar{F} = (\bar{A} + \bar{B})(\bar{C} + \bar{D})\).

front: A three-variable function is \(F(A,B,C) = \sum m(0,2,4,6)\). Use a Karnaugh map to find the minimal expression.
explanation: With \(A\) as the MSB and \(C\) as the LSB, the minterms are \(m_0 = \bar{A}\bar{B}\bar{C}\), \(m_2 = \bar{A}B\bar{C}\), \(m_4 = A\bar{B}\bar{C}\), \(m_6 = AB\bar{C}\); all have \(C = 0\). They combine into one group covering every cell where \(C = 0\), so \(F = \bar{C}\).

front: Minimize the four-variable function \(F(A,B,C,D) = \sum m(0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11)\) using a Karnaugh map.
explanation: Using place values \(A=8,\ B=4,\ C=2,\ D=1\), every listed minterm has \(B = 0\): minterms 0, 1, 2, 3 have \(A=0\) and \(B=0\); minterms 8, 9, 10, 11 have \(A=1\) and \(B=0\). The eight cells form a single group in which \(A\), \(C\), and \(D\) each take both values, leaving only \(B = 0\) common, so \(F = \bar{B}\).

front: A JK flip-flop currently stores \(Q = 1\). Inputs \(J = 1\) and \(K = 1\) are applied. What is \(Q\) after the next active clock edge?
explanation: When \(J = K = 1\), the JK flip-flop is in toggle mode, so \(Q_{\text{next}} = \bar{Q}\). With the present state \(Q = 1\), the next state is \(Q_{\text{next}} = 0\).

front: A 4-bit binary ripple (asynchronous) counter is clocked at \(16\ \text{MHz}\). What is the frequency at the most-significant output \(Q_3\)?
explanation: Each stage of a ripple counter toggles at half the rate of the previous stage, so a 4-bit counter divides the clock by \(2^4 = 16\). Thus \(f_{Q_3} = \dfrac{16\ \text{MHz}}{16} = 1\ \text{MHz}\).

front: A full adder receives \(A = 1\), \(B = 1\), and carry-in \(C_{in} = 1\). Find the sum bit \(S\) and carry-out \(C_{out}\).
explanation: For a full adder, \(S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in} = 1\oplus 1\oplus 1 = 1\) and \(C_{out} = AB + BC_{in} + AC_{in} = 1\). This agrees with \(1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = 11_2\): a sum bit of 1 with a carry of 1.

front: The two inputs of a 2-input NAND gate are tied together and driven by a single signal \(A\). What single-gate function results?
explanation: With both inputs equal to \(A\), the output is \(F = \overline{A\cdot A} = \bar{A}\), since \(A\cdot A = A\). The gate therefore inverts its input, functioning as a NOT gate.

front: Two point charges \( Q_1 = 2\ \mu\text{C} \) and \( Q_2 = 3\ \mu\text{C} \) are separated by \( 30\ \text{cm} \) in free space. Find the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them.
explanation: Use Coulomb's law \( F = \dfrac{k Q_1 Q_2}{r^{2}} \) with \( k \approx 8.99\times10^{9}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2} \). Substitute \( r = 0.30\ \text{m} \): \( F = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(2\times10^{-6})(3\times10^{-6})}{(0.30)^{2}} \). The numerator is \( 5.39\times10^{-2} \) and \( (0.30)^{2} = 0.09 \), so \( F \approx 0.60\ \text{N} \).

front: Find the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of \( 2\ \text{m} \) from a \( +10\ \text{nC} \) point charge in free space.
explanation: The field of a point charge is \( E = \dfrac{kQ}{r^{2}} \) with \( k \approx 8.99\times10^{9}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2} \). Substitute \( Q = 10\times10^{-9}\ \text{C} \) and \( r = 2\ \text{m} \): \( E = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(10\times10^{-9})}{2^{2}} = \dfrac{89.9}{4} \). Therefore \( E \approx 22.5\ \text{V/m} \), directed radially outward.

front: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area \( 0.02\ \text{m}^{2} \) and plate separation \( 1\ \text{mm} \), filled with a dielectric of relative permittivity \( \varepsilon_r = 4 \). Find its capacitance.
explanation: Parallel-plate capacitance is \( C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r A}{d} \) with \( \varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\ \text{F/m} \). Substitute \( A = 0.02\ \text{m}^{2} \), \( d = 1\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} \), and \( \varepsilon_r = 4 \): \( C = \dfrac{(8.854\times10^{-12})(4)(0.02)}{1\times10^{-3}} \). This gives \( C \approx 7.08\times10^{-10}\ \text{F} = 708\ \text{pF} \).

front: A \( 10\ \mu\text{F} \) capacitor is charged to \( 50\ \text{V} \). Find the energy stored in the capacitor.
explanation: The energy stored in a capacitor is \( W = \tfrac{1}{2} C V^{2} \). Substitute \( C = 10\times10^{-6}\ \text{F} \) and \( V = 50\ \text{V} \): \( W = \tfrac{1}{2}(10\times10^{-6})(50)^{2} \). Since \( (50)^{2} = 2500 \), \( W = \tfrac{1}{2}(10\times10^{-6})(2500) = 1.25\times10^{-2}\ \text{J} = 12.5\ \text{mJ} \).

front: A long straight wire in air carries a current of \( 10\ \text{A} \). Find the magnetic flux density at a radial distance of \( 5\ \text{cm} \) from the wire.
explanation: For a long straight wire, Ampere's law gives \( B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \) with \( \mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{H/m} \). Substitute \( I = 10\ \text{A} \) and \( r = 0.05\ \text{m} \): \( B = \dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(10)}{2\pi(0.05)} \). This simplifies to \( B = \dfrac{(2\times10^{-7})(10)}{0.05} = 4\times10^{-5}\ \text{T} = 40\ \mu\text{T} \).

front: A straight conductor of length \( 0.5\ \text{m} \) carries a current of \( 4\ \text{A} \) perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of \( 0.8\ \text{T} \). Find the magnitude of the force on the conductor.
explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor is \( F = B I L \sin\theta \). The current is perpendicular to the field, so \( \theta = 90^{\circ} \) and \( \sin\theta = 1 \). Substitute the values: \( F = (0.8)(4)(0.5)(1) = 1.6\ \text{N} \).

front: The magnetic flux through a \( 100 \)-turn coil changes uniformly from \( 2\ \text{mWb} \) to \( 10\ \text{mWb} \) in \( 4\ \text{ms} \). Find the magnitude of the induced EMF.
explanation: Faraday's law gives \( |\mathcal{E}| = N\left|\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right| \). Here \( \Delta\Phi = 10 - 2 = 8\ \text{mWb} = 8\times10^{-3}\ \text{Wb} \) and \( \Delta t = 4\times10^{-3}\ \text{s} \). Thus \( |\mathcal{E}| = 100 \times \dfrac{8\times10^{-3}}{4\times10^{-3}} = 100 \times 2 = 200\ \text{V} \).

front: A lossless transmission line has a distributed inductance of \( 250\ \text{nH/m} \) and a distributed capacitance of \( 100\ \text{pF/m} \). Find the characteristic impedance of the line.
explanation: For a lossless line, \( Z_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}} \). Substitute \( L = 250\times10^{-9}\ \text{H/m} \) and \( C = 100\times10^{-12}\ \text{F/m} \): \( \dfrac{L}{C} = \dfrac{250\times10^{-9}}{100\times10^{-12}} = 2500 \). Therefore \( Z_0 = \sqrt{2500} = 50\ \Omega \).

front: A \( 50\ \Omega \) transmission line is terminated with a \( 75\ \Omega \) resistive load. Find the voltage reflection coefficient at the load.
explanation: The reflection coefficient is \( \Gamma = \dfrac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0} \). Substitute \( Z_L = 75\ \Omega \) and \( Z_0 = 50\ \Omega \): \( \Gamma = \dfrac{75 - 50}{75 + 50} = \dfrac{25}{125} \). Therefore \( \Gamma = 0.2 \) (real and positive).

front: An electromagnetic wave propagates in free space at a frequency of \( 3\ \text{GHz} \). Find its wavelength. (Use \( c = 3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \).)
explanation: Wavelength and frequency are related by \( \lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} \). Substitute \( c = 3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \) and \( f = 3\times10^{9}\ \text{Hz} \): \( \lambda = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{3\times10^{9}} \). Therefore \( \lambda = 0.1\ \text{m} = 10\ \text{cm} \).

front: A uniform plane wave propagates in a lossless, nonmagnetic dielectric with relative permittivity \( \varepsilon_r = 4 \). Find the phase velocity of the wave. (Use \( c = 3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \).)
explanation: In a nonmagnetic medium (\( \mu_r = 1 \)), the phase velocity is \( v_p = \dfrac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}} \). Substitute \( \varepsilon_r = 4 \): \( v_p = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{\sqrt{4}} = \dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{2} \). Therefore \( v_p = 1.5\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \).

front: Find the intrinsic (wave) impedance of a lossless, nonmagnetic medium with relative permittivity \( \varepsilon_r = 4 \). Use the free-space intrinsic impedance \( \eta_0 \approx 377\ \Omega \).
explanation: For a nonmagnetic medium, \( \eta = \dfrac{\eta_0}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}} \). Substitute \( \eta_0 = 377\ \Omega \) and \( \varepsilon_r = 4 \): \( \eta = \dfrac{377}{\sqrt{4}} = \dfrac{377}{2} \). Therefore \( \eta \approx 188.5\ \Omega \).

front: A long air-core solenoid has \( 500 \) turns wound uniformly over a length of \( 25\ \text{cm} \) and carries \( 2\ \text{A} \). Find the magnetic flux density near the center of the solenoid.
explanation: Inside a long solenoid, \( B = \mu_0 n I \), where \( n = N/\ell \) is the number of turns per unit length. Here \( n = \dfrac{500}{0.25} = 2000\ \text{turns/m} \). Then \( B = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(2000)(2) \approx 5.03\times10^{-3}\ \text{T} = 5.03\ \text{mT} \).

front: An infinite line charge in free space has a uniform linear charge density of \( 5\ \text{nC/m} \). Find the magnitude of the electric field at a radial distance of \( 10\ \text{cm} \).
explanation: For an infinite line charge, \( E = \dfrac{\rho_\ell}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \dfrac{2k\rho_\ell}{r} \) with \( k \approx 8.99\times10^{9} \). Substitute \( \rho_\ell = 5\times10^{-9}\ \text{C/m} \) and \( r = 0.10\ \text{m} \): \( E = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(5\times10^{-9})}{0.10} \). Therefore \( E \approx 899\ \text{V/m} \).

front: A uniform plane wave in free space has a frequency of \( 150\ \text{MHz} \). Find its phase constant \( \beta \). (Use \( c = 3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \).)
explanation: The phase constant is \( \beta = \dfrac{\omega}{c} = \dfrac{2\pi f}{c} \). Substitute \( f = 150\times10^{6}\ \text{Hz} \): \( \beta = \dfrac{2\pi(150\times10^{6})}{3\times10^{8}} = 2\pi(0.5) \). Therefore \( \beta = \pi \approx 3.14\ \text{rad/m} \).

front: A full-wave bridge rectifier is driven by a transformer secondary with peak voltage \(V_m = 18\ \text{V}\). The four rectifier diodes are silicon with a \(0.7\ \text{V}\) drop each. Find the peak voltage delivered to the load.
explanation: In a bridge rectifier, two diodes conduct in series on each half-cycle, so two forward drops are subtracted. \[V_{L,\text{peak}} = V_m - 2V_D = 18 - 2(0.7) = 16.6\ \text{V}.\]

front: A light-emitting diode with forward drop \(V_F = 2\ \text{V}\) is to operate at \(I = 15\ \text{mA}\) from a \(5\ \text{V}\) supply using a series current-limiting resistor. Find the required resistance.
explanation: The series resistor drops the difference between the supply and the LED voltage while carrying the LED current. \[R = \frac{V_S - V_F}{I} = \frac{5 - 2}{0.015} = 200\ \Omega.\]

front: A \(5\ \text{V}\) Zener shunt regulator is fed from a \(15\ \text{V}\) source through a series resistor \(R_s = 200\ \Omega\) and drives a load \(R_L = 1\ \text{k}\Omega\). Assuming the diode maintains \(5\ \text{V}\), find the current in the Zener diode.
explanation: Current through the series resistor: \[I_{R_s} = \frac{15 - 5}{200} = 50\ \text{mA}.\] Load current: \[I_L = \frac{5}{1000} = 5\ \text{mA}.\] KCL at the regulator node gives \[I_Z = I_{R_s} - I_L = 50 - 5 = 45\ \text{mA}.\]

front: A \(5\ \text{V}\) Zener diode in a shunt regulator carries \(45\ \text{mA}\). Find the power dissipated in the diode.
explanation: Power dissipated equals the diode voltage times its current. \[P_Z = V_Z I_Z = (5)(0.045) = 0.225\ \text{W} = 225\ \text{mW}.\]

front: A full-wave rectifier operating from a \(60\ \text{Hz}\) line uses a capacitor filter \(C = 1000\ \mu\text{F}\) and supplies a load drawing \(I_L = 100\ \text{mA}\). Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple voltage.
explanation: For a full-wave rectifier the capacitor is recharged twice per line cycle, so the ripple frequency is \(f_r = 2(60) = 120\ \text{Hz}\). \[V_{r(pp)} \approx \frac{I_L}{f_r C} = \frac{0.1}{(120)(1000\times10^{-6})} = 0.83\ \text{V}.\]

front: A silicon BJT with \(\beta = 100\) and \(V_{BE} = 0.7\ \text{V}\) uses fixed base bias: \(V_{CC} = 10\ \text{V}\) connects to the base through \(R_B = 465\ \text{k}\Omega\). Find the base current and the collector current.
explanation: Base loop (KVL): \[I_B = \frac{V_{CC} - V_{BE}}{R_B} = \frac{10 - 0.7}{465\times10^{3}} = 20\ \mu\text{A}.\] In the active region, \[I_C = \beta I_B = 100(20\ \mu\text{A}) = 2\ \text{mA}.\]

front: A BJT voltage-divider bias circuit has \(V_{CC} = 12\ \text{V}\), \(R_1 = 40\ \text{k}\Omega\) (from \(V_{CC}\) to base), \(R_2 = 20\ \text{k}\Omega\) (base to ground), \(R_C = 2\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_E = 1\ \text{k}\Omega\), and \(V_{BE} = 0.7\ \text{V}\). Neglecting base current, find \(I_C\) and \(V_{CE}\).
explanation: Divider (base) voltage: \[V_B = V_{CC}\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2} = 12\cdot\frac{20}{60} = 4\ \text{V}.\] Emitter voltage and current: \[V_E = V_B - V_{BE} = 3.3\ \text{V},\quad I_C \approx I_E = \frac{3.3}{1000} = 3.3\ \text{mA}.\] Collector-emitter loop: \[V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C(R_C + R_E) = 12 - (3.3\ \text{mA})(3\ \text{k}\Omega) = 2.1\ \text{V}.\]

front: The common-base current gain of a BJT is \(\alpha = 0.98\). Find the common-emitter current gain \(\beta\).
explanation: The current gains are related by \[\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha} = \frac{0.98}{1 - 0.98} = \frac{0.98}{0.02} = 49.\]

front: An NMOS transistor operating in saturation has \(k_n'\,(W/L) = 1\ \text{mA/V}^2\) and threshold voltage \(V_t = 1\ \text{V}\). If \(V_{GS} = 3\ \text{V}\), find the drain current.
explanation: Saturation drain current: \[I_D = \tfrac{1}{2}k_n'\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS} - V_t)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1\ \text{mA/V}^2)(3 - 1)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1\ \text{mA/V}^2)(4\ \text{V}^2) = 2\ \text{mA}.\]

front: An NMOS device with \(k_n'\,(W/L) = 0.5\ \text{mA/V}^2\) and \(V_t = 1\ \text{V}\) has \(V_{GS} = 3\ \text{V}\), a drain supply \(V_{DD} = 10\ \text{V}\), and drain resistor \(R_D = 2\ \text{k}\Omega\) (source grounded). Find \(I_D\) and \(V_{DS}\), and verify the operating region.
explanation: Assume saturation: \[I_D = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.5\ \text{mA/V}^2)(3 - 1)^2 = 1\ \text{mA}.\] Drain voltage: \[V_{DS} = V_{DD} - I_D R_D = 10 - (1\ \text{mA})(2\ \text{k}\Omega) = 8\ \text{V}.\] Since \(V_{DS} = 8\ \text{V} \ge V_{GS} - V_t = 2\ \text{V}\), the transistor is in saturation, confirming the assumption.

front: An ideal op-amp is configured as an inverting amplifier with feedback resistor \(R_f = 120\ \text{k}\Omega\) and input resistor \(R_{\text{in}} = 20\ \text{k}\Omega\). For an input of \(0.5\ \text{V}\), find the output voltage.
explanation: Inverting closed-loop gain: \[A_v = -\frac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}}} = -\frac{120}{20} = -6.\] Output voltage: \[V_{out} = A_v V_{in} = -6(0.5) = -3\ \text{V}.\]

front: An ideal op-amp non-inverting amplifier has feedback resistor \(R_f = 90\ \text{k}\Omega\) and a grounded resistor \(R_1 = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\). For an input of \(0.4\ \text{V}\), find the output voltage.
explanation: Non-inverting closed-loop gain: \[A_v = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1} = 1 + \frac{90}{10} = 10.\] Output voltage: \[V_{out} = A_v V_{in} = 10(0.4) = 4\ \text{V}.\]

front: An ideal inverting summing amplifier has feedback resistor \(R_f = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\). Its inputs are \(V_1 = 1\ \text{V}\) through \(R_1 = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\) and \(V_2 = 2\ \text{V}\) through \(R_2 = 5\ \text{k}\Omega\). Find the output voltage.
explanation: Summing the input currents at the virtual-ground node: \[V_{out} = -R_f\left(\frac{V_1}{R_1} + \frac{V_2}{R_2}\right) = -(10\ \text{k}\Omega)\left(\frac{1}{10\ \text{k}\Omega} + \frac{2}{5\ \text{k}\Omega}\right).\] \[V_{out} = -(10\ \text{k}\Omega)(0.1\ \text{mA} + 0.4\ \text{mA}) = -5\ \text{V}.\]

front: A BJT is biased at \(I_C = 1\ \text{mA}\) with \(\beta = 100\) and thermal voltage \(V_T = 25\ \text{mV}\). Find the small-signal transconductance \(g_m\) and the base input resistance \(r_\pi\).
explanation: Transconductance: \[g_m = \frac{I_C}{V_T} = \frac{1\ \text{mA}}{25\ \text{mV}} = 40\ \text{mA/V}.\] Input resistance: \[r_\pi = \frac{\beta}{g_m} = \frac{100}{0.04\ \text{S}} = 2500\ \Omega = 2.5\ \text{k}\Omega.\]

front: A common-emitter amplifier has transconductance \(g_m = 25\ \text{mA/V}\) and collector resistor \(R_C = 8\ \text{k}\Omega\), with \(r_o \gg R_C\) and no emitter degeneration. Find the mid-band small-signal voltage gain.
explanation: The common-emitter mid-band voltage gain is the product of transconductance and collector resistance: \[A_v = -g_m R_C = -(0.025\ \text{S})(8000\ \Omega) = -200.\] The minus sign reflects the \(180^\circ\) phase inversion of the stage.

front: An NMOS transistor in saturation has \(k_n'\,(W/L) = 2\ \text{mA/V}^2\) and is biased at an overdrive voltage \(V_{OV} = V_{GS} - V_t = 1\ \text{V}\). Find its small-signal transconductance \(g_m\).
explanation: For a MOSFET in saturation the transconductance is \[g_m = k_n'\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS} - V_t) = (2\ \text{mA/V}^2)(1\ \text{V}) = 2\ \text{mA/V}.\]

front: A forward-biased diode carries a DC current \(I_D = 0.5\ \text{mA}\). With ideality factor \(n = 1\) and thermal voltage \(V_T = 25\ \text{mV}\), find the diode's small-signal (dynamic) resistance.
explanation: The dynamic resistance is the reciprocal of the slope of the diode I-V curve at the operating point: \[r_d = \frac{n V_T}{I_D} = \frac{(1)(25\ \text{mV})}{0.5\ \text{mA}} = 50\ \Omega.\]

front: An ideal op-amp difference amplifier is built with matched resistor ratios \(R_f/R_1 = 5\) on both the inverting and non-inverting sides. The inputs are \(V_1 = 1.2\ \text{V}\) (inverting) and \(V_2 = 1.5\ \text{V}\) (non-inverting). Find the output voltage.
explanation: For a balanced difference amplifier the output depends only on the input difference: \[V_{out} = \frac{R_f}{R_1}(V_2 - V_1) = 5(1.5 - 1.2) = 5(0.3) = 1.5\ \text{V}.\]

front: An engineer deposits \(\text{\$8{,}000}\) in an account earning \(6\%\) compounded annually. What is the account worth after \(10\) years?
explanation: 1) Use the single-payment compound-amount factor \((F/P, i, n) = (1+i)^n\). 2) \((1.06)^{10} = 1.7908\). 3) \(F = P(1+i)^n = \text{\$8{,}000}\times 1.7908 \approx \text{\$14{,}327}\).

front: How much must be deposited today in an account earning \(8\%\) compounded annually to grow to \(\text{\$50{,}000}\) in \(15\) years?
A new machine is expected to save \(\text{\$12{,}000}\) per year for \(8\) years. At an interest rate of \(10\%\), what is the present worth of these savings?
A \(\text{\$30{,}000}\) loan is repaid in equal end-of-year payments over \(5\) years at an interest rate of \(9\%\). What is the annual payment?
\(\text{\$5{,}000}\) is deposited at the end of each year for \(12\) years into an account earning \(7\%\) compounded annually. What is the future worth of the deposits?
How much must be deposited at the end of each year to accumulate \(\text{\$100{,}000}\) in \(10\) years, if the account earns \(6\%\) compounded annually?

Maintenance on a generator costs \(\text{\$1{,}000}\) at the end of year \(1\) and increases by \(\text{\$200}\) each year through year \(5\). At \(10\%\) interest, what is the present worth of the maintenance costs?

A cash flow is \(\text{\$0}\) in year \(1\) and increases by \(\text{\$500}\) each year through year \(6\) (that is, \(\text{\$0}, \text{\$500}, \ldots, \text{\$2{,}500}\)). At \(8\%\) interest, what equivalent uniform annual amount is this series worth?
explanation: 1) A pure arithmetic gradient converts to a uniform series with \((A/G, i, n) = \dfrac{1}{i} - \dfrac{n}{(1+i)^n - 1}\). 2) \((A/G, 8\%, 6) = \dfrac{1}{0.08} - \dfrac{6}{(1.08)^6 - 1} = 12.5 - 10.224 = 2.2763\). 3) \(A = G(A/G, 8\%, 6) = \text{\$500}\times 2.2763 \approx \text{\$1{,}138}\).

front: A credit card charges a nominal annual interest rate of \(18\%\) compounded monthly. What is the effective annual interest rate?
explanation: 1) Effective annual rate: \(i_{\text{eff}} = \left(1 + \dfrac{r}{m}\right)^m - 1\) with \(r = 0.18\), \(m = 12\). 2) \(i_{\text{eff}} = \left(1 + \dfrac{0.18}{12}\right)^{12} - 1 = (1.015)^{12} - 1\). 3) \(i_{\text{eff}} = 1.1956 - 1 \approx 19.56\%\).

front: An investment of \(\text{\$10{,}000}\) today returns a single lump sum of \(\text{\$16{,}105}\) at the end of \(5\) years. What annual rate of return does it earn?

A machine costs \(\text{\$60{,}000}\), has a salvage value of \(\text{\$10{,}000}\), and a useful life of \(5\) years. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the book value at the end of year \(3\)?
explanation: 1) Straight-line annual depreciation: \(D = \dfrac{\text{cost} - \text{salvage}}{n} = \dfrac{\text{\$60{,}000} - \text{\$10{,}000}}{5} = \text{\$10{,}000}\) per year. 2) Accumulated depreciation after \(3\) years \(= 3\times\text{\$10{,}000} = \text{\$30{,}000}\). 3) \(BV_3 = \text{\$60{,}000} - \text{\$30{,}000} = \text{\$30{,}000}\).

front: A \(\text{\$40{,}000}\) asset has a \(5\)-year depreciable life. Using the double-declining-balance (\(200\%\) DB) method, what is the depreciation charge in year \(2\)?
explanation: 1) Double-declining-balance rate: \(d = \dfrac{2}{n} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.40\), applied to the beginning-of-year book value. 2) Year 1: \(D_1 = 0.40\times\text{\$40{,}000} = \text{\$16{,}000}\), so \(BV_1 = \text{\$24{,}000}\). 3) Year 2: \(D_2 = 0.40\times\text{\$24{,}000} = \text{\$9{,}600}\).

front: A highway project has a present worth of user benefits of \(\text{\$5{,}000{,}000}\), present-worth disbenefits of \(\text{\$500{,}000}\), and a present worth of costs of \(\text{\$3{,}000{,}000}\). Using the conventional benefit-cost ratio, is the project justified?
explanation: 1) The conventional benefit-cost ratio nets disbenefits against benefits: \(B/C = \dfrac{\text{benefits} - \text{disbenefits}}{\text{costs}}\). 2) \(B/C = \dfrac{\text{\$5{,}000{,}000} - \text{\$500{,}000}}{\text{\$3{,}000{,}000}} = \dfrac{\text{\$4{,}500{,}000}}{\text{\$3{,}000{,}000}} = 1.5\). 3) Since \(1.5 > 1\), the project is economically justified.

front: A monument costs \(\text{\$2{,}000{,}000}\) to construct and \(\text{\$40{,}000}\) per year to maintain in perpetuity. At an interest rate of \(4\%\), what is its capitalized cost?
explanation: 1) Capitalized cost is the first cost plus the present worth of perpetual annual costs: \(CC = P_0 + \dfrac{A}{i}\). 2) \(\dfrac{A}{i} = \dfrac{\text{\$40{,}000}}{0.04} = \text{\$1{,}000{,}000}\). 3) \(CC = \text{\$2{,}000{,}000} + \text{\$1{,}000{,}000} = \text{\$3{,}000{,}000}\).

front: A scholarship fund will pay \(\text{\$10{,}000}\) per year for \(4\) years, with the first payment at the end of year \(6\) (payments in years \(6, 7, 8, 9\)). At \(8\%\) interest, what single amount today is equivalent to the fund?
explanation: 1) Value the 4-payment annuity one period before its first payment (end of year \(5\)) with \((P/A, 8\%, 4) = 3.3121\): \(P_5 = \text{\$10{,}000}\times 3.3121 = \text{\$33{,}121}\). 2) Discount back \(5\) years with \((P/F, 8\%, 5) = 0.6806\). 3) \(P_0 = \text{\$33{,}121}\times 0.6806 \approx \text{\$22{,}542}\).

front: A \(1500\ \text{kg}\) car travels in a straight line at \(20\ \text{m/s}\). Determine its kinetic energy.

A hoist motor raises a \(200\ \text{kg}\) load at constant speed to a height of \(15\ \text{m}\) in \(10\ \text{s}\). Neglecting losses, find the average mechanical power delivered. Use \(g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^{2}\).
explanation: Work done against gravity: \(W = mgh = (200)(9.81)(15) = 29{,}430\ \text{J}\). Power is work per unit time: \(P = W/t = 29{,}430/10 = 2943\ \text{W} \approx 2.94\ \text{kW}\).

front: A constant force of \(50\ \text{N}\) is applied at \(30^{\circ}\) above the horizontal to drag a crate \(8\ \text{m}\) horizontally. How much work does this force do on the crate?
explanation: Only the force component along the displacement does work: \(W = F d \cos\theta\). Substitute \(F = 50\ \text{N}\), \(d = 8\ \text{m}\), \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\): \(W = (50)(8)\cos 30^{\circ} = 400 \times 0.866 \approx 346\ \text{J}\).

front: A vehicle moves at a steady \(25\ \text{m/s}\) while its drivetrain provides a constant tractive force of \(800\ \text{N}\). Determine the power output.
explanation: For a force acting along the direction of motion, power is \(P = F v\). Substitute \(F = 800\ \text{N}\) and \(v = 25\ \text{m/s}\): \(P = (800)(25) = 20{,}000\ \text{W} = 20\ \text{kW}\).

front: A \(1500\ \text{W}\) electric motor runs continuously for \(4\ \text{hours}\). How much electrical energy does it consume, expressed in \(\text{kWh}\) and in \(\text{MJ}\)?
explanation: Energy is power times time: \(E = P t = (1.5\ \text{kW})(4\ \text{h}) = 6\ \text{kWh}\). Convert with \(1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6\ \text{MJ}\): \(E = 6 \times 3.6 = 21.6\ \text{MJ}\).

front: An electric heater connected to a \(240\ \text{V}\) supply draws \(8\ \text{A}\). Determine the power it dissipates and the total charge that flows through it in \(5\ \text{minutes}\).
explanation: Power delivered to the load: \(P = VI = (240)(8) = 1920\ \text{W}\). Charge is current times time, with \(t = 5\ \text{min} = 300\ \text{s}\): \(Q = I t = (8)(300) = 2400\ \text{C}\).

front: The charge passing a point in a wire is \(q(t) = 3t^{2} + 2t\) coulombs, with \(t\) in seconds. Find the current at \(t = 2\ \text{s}\).
explanation: Current is the time derivative of charge: \(i(t) = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = 6t + 2\). Evaluate at \(t = 2\ \text{s}\): \(i(2) = 6(2) + 2 = 14\ \text{A}\).

front: Two forces act at a single point: \(30\ \text{N}\) directed east and \(40\ \text{N}\) directed north. Find the magnitude and direction (measured from east) of the resultant.
explanation: Perpendicular components combine by the Pythagorean theorem: \(R = \sqrt{30^{2} + 40^{2}} = \sqrt{900 + 1600} = \sqrt{2500} = 50\ \text{N}\). Direction: \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(40/30) = \tan^{-1}(1.333) \approx 53.1^{\circ}\).

front: A wrench \(0.40\ \text{m}\) long has a \(150\ \text{N}\) force applied at its far end, directed perpendicular to the handle. Determine the moment (torque) about the bolt.
explanation: The moment of a force about a point is \(M = F d\) when the force is perpendicular to the moment arm. Substitute \(F = 150\ \text{N}\) and \(d = 0.40\ \text{m}\): \(M = (150)(0.40) = 60\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}\).

front: A constant net force of \(50\ \text{N}\) acts on a \(10\ \text{kg}\) block initially at rest on a frictionless surface. Find its acceleration, its speed after \(4\ \text{s}\), and the distance travelled in that time.
explanation: Newton's second law: \(a = F/m = 50/10 = 5\ \text{m/s}^{2}\). Starting from rest, \(v = at = (5)(4) = 20\ \text{m/s}\). Distance: \(d = \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(5)(4)^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(5)(16) = 40\ \text{m}\).

front: An object is released from rest and falls \(20\ \text{m}\) with negligible air resistance. Find its speed just before impact and the time of fall. Use \(g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^{2}\).

A \(0.15\ \text{kg}\) baseball is struck so that its speed changes from \(0\) to \(40\ \text{m/s}\) during a \(0.010\ \text{s}\) contact. Find the impulse delivered to the ball and the average force during contact.
explanation: Impulse equals the change in momentum: \(J = m\,\Delta v = (0.15)(40 - 0) = 6\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s} = 6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}\). Average force: \(F_{avg} = J/\Delta t = 6/0.010 = 600\ \text{N}\).

front: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of \(2\ \text{kg}\) of water from \(20\,^{\circ}\text{C}\) to \(80\,^{\circ}\text{C}\)? Take the specific heat of water as \(4186\ \text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}\).
explanation: Sensible heat: \(Q = m c \Delta T\), with \(\Delta T = 80 - 20 = 60\ \text{K}\). Substitute: \(Q = (2)(4186)(60) = 502{,}320\ \text{J} \approx 502\ \text{kJ}\).

front: A heat engine absorbs \(800\ \text{J}\) from a hot reservoir and rejects \(500\ \text{J}\) to a cold reservoir each cycle. Determine its thermal efficiency.
explanation: Net work per cycle: \(W = Q_H - Q_C = 800 - 500 = 300\ \text{J}\). Thermal efficiency: \(\eta = W/Q_H = 300/800 = 0.375 = 37.5\%\).

front: A power cycle operates between thermal reservoirs at \(600\ \text{K}\) and \(300\ \text{K}\). What is the maximum possible (Carnot) thermal efficiency?
explanation: Carnot efficiency depends only on the absolute reservoir temperatures: \(\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \dfrac{T_C}{T_H}\). Substitute \(T_C = 300\ \text{K}\), \(T_H = 600\ \text{K}\): \(\eta = 1 - 300/600 = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5 = 50\%\).

front: In a well-insulated container, \(1\ \text{kg}\) of water at \(80\,^{\circ}\text{C}\) is mixed with \(3\ \text{kg}\) of water at \(20\,^{\circ}\text{C}\). Assuming no heat loss, find the final equilibrium temperature.
explanation: Energy balance (heat lost by hot water equals heat gained by cold water); the specific heats cancel: \(m_1(T_1 - T_f) = m_2(T_f - T_2)\). So \(1(80 - T_f) = 3(T_f - 20)\), giving \(80 - T_f = 3T_f - 60\). Then \(140 = 4T_f\), so \(T_f = 35\,^{\circ}\text{C}\).

front: At steady state, a mixer receives \(2\ \text{kg/s}\) of brine containing \(10\%\) salt by mass and \(3\ \text{kg/s}\) of pure water. Find the salt mass fraction of the combined outlet stream.
explanation: Overall mass balance: outlet flow \(= 2 + 3 = 5\ \text{kg/s}\). Salt (species) balance: salt in \(= 0.10(2) + 0(3) = 0.2\ \text{kg/s}\). Outlet mass fraction \(= 0.2/5 = 0.04 = 4\%\).

front: Two point charges \(Q_1 = 2\ \mu\text{C}\) and \(Q_2 = 3\ \mu\text{C}\) are \(0.10\ \text{m}\) apart in air. Find the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. Use \(k = 8.99\times10^{9}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}\).
explanation: Coulomb's law gives \(F = \dfrac{k Q_1 Q_2}{r^{2}}\). Substituting, \(F = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(2\times10^{-6})(3\times10^{-6})}{(0.10)^{2}} = \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times 6\times10^{-12}}{0.01} \approx 5.39\ \text{N}\).

front: An electron is moved through a potential difference of \(50\ \text{V}\). How much work is done on it? Use \(e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\).
explanation: The work to move a charge through a potential difference is \(W = qV\). Substituting the electron charge magnitude, \(W = (1.602\times10^{-19})(50) = 8.01\times10^{-18}\ \text{J}\), equivalently \(50\ \text{eV}\).

front: Two large parallel plates are separated by \(2\ \text{mm}\) with \(100\ \text{V}\) applied across them. Assuming a uniform field, find the electric field strength between the plates.
explanation: For a uniform field between parallel plates, \(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\). Substituting \(V = 100\ \text{V}\) and \(d = 2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}\): \(E = \dfrac{100}{0.002} = 50{,}000\ \text{V/m} = 5\times10^{4}\ \text{V/m}\).

front: A \(5\ \mu\text{C}\) point charge is placed in a uniform electric field of \(2000\ \text{V/m}\). Find the magnitude of the force on the charge.
explanation: The force on a charge in an electric field is \(F = qE\). Substituting, \(F = (5\times10^{-6})(2000) = 0.01\ \text{N}\).

front: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area \(0.02\ \text{m}^{2}\) and plate separation \(1\ \text{mm}\) with a vacuum dielectric. Find its capacitance. Use \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{F/m}\).
explanation: The parallel-plate capacitance is \(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\). Substituting, \(C = \dfrac{(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.02)}{0.001} = 1.77\times10^{-10}\ \text{F} \approx 177\ \text{pF}\).

front: A \(10\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is charged to \(12\ \text{V}\). How much charge is stored on it?
explanation: The charge on a capacitor is \(Q = CV\). Substituting, \(Q = (10\times10^{-6})(12) = 1.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{C} = 120\ \mu\text{C}\).

front: Find the energy stored in a \(100\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor charged to \(50\ \text{V}\).
explanation: The energy stored in a capacitor is \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}\). Substituting, \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(100\times10^{-6})(50)^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(100\times10^{-6})(2500) = 0.125\ \text{J}\).

front: Find the energy stored in a \(200\ \text{mH}\) inductor carrying a steady current of \(3\ \text{A}\).
explanation: The energy stored in an inductor is \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^{2}\). Substituting, \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.200)(3)^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.200)(9) = 0.9\ \text{J}\).

front: The current through a \(50\ \text{mH}\) inductor increases uniformly from \(0\) to \(2\ \text{A}\) in \(10\ \text{ms}\). Find the voltage across the inductor during this interval.
explanation: The inductor voltage is \(v = L\dfrac{di}{dt}\). For a uniform ramp, \(\dfrac{di}{dt} = \dfrac{2 - 0}{10\times10^{-3}} = 200\ \text{A/s}\). Thus \(v = (0.050)(200) = 10\ \text{V}\).

front: A straight wire \(0.5\ \text{m}\) long carries a current of \(4\ \text{A}\) perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of \(0.3\ \text{T}\). Find the magnitude of the force on the wire.
explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor is \(F = BIL\sin\theta\). With \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\), \(\sin\theta = 1\), so \(F = (0.3)(4)(0.5) = 0.6\ \text{N}\).

front: A proton (\(q = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\)) moves at \(1\times10^{6}\ \text{m/s}\) perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of \(0.5\ \text{T}\). Find the magnitude of the magnetic force on it.
explanation: The magnetic force on a moving charge is \(F = qvB\sin\theta\). With \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\), \(F = (1.602\times10^{-19})(1\times10^{6})(0.5) = 8.01\times10^{-14}\ \text{N}\).

front: A spring of stiffness \(k = 400\ \text{N/m}\) is stretched \(0.05\ \text{m}\) from its natural length. Find the elastic potential energy stored.
explanation: The elastic (strain) energy stored in a linear spring is \(U = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}\). Substituting, \(U = \tfrac{1}{2}(400)(0.05)^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}(400)(0.0025) = 0.5\ \text{J}\).

front: A \(4\ \Omega\) resistor carries a steady current of \(3\ \text{A}\) for \(2\ \text{minutes}\). How much heat energy is dissipated?
explanation: The power dissipated is \(P = I^{2}R = (3)^{2}(4) = 36\ \text{W}\). Energy is power times time, with \(t = 2\ \text{min} = 120\ \text{s}\): \(E = Pt = 36 \times 120 = 4320\ \text{J}\).

front: A steel rod \(2\ \text{m}\) long is heated so that its temperature rises by \(50\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\). If the coefficient of linear thermal expansion is \(\alpha = 1.2\times10^{-5}\ /^{\circ}\text{C}\), find the increase in length.
explanation: The thermal expansion of a rod is \(\Delta L = \alpha L\,\Delta T\). Substituting, \(\Delta L = (1.2\times10^{-5})(2)(50) = 1.2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 1.2\ \text{mm}\).

front: How much heat is required to completely melt \(0.5\ \text{kg}\) of ice at \(0\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\)? The latent heat of fusion of water is \(L_f = 3.34\times10^{5}\ \text{J/kg}\).
explanation: For a phase change at constant temperature, \(Q = mL_f\). Substituting, \(Q = (0.5)(3.34\times10^{5}) = 1.67\times10^{5}\ \text{J} = 167\ \text{kJ}\).

front: A client pressures a design engineer to lower a structure's load safety factor below the governing code minimum to cut cost, arguing it 'will likely never see full load.' What is the engineer's ethical obligation?
back: Refuse to go below the code-required safety factor; protecting public safety is paramount and cannot be traded for cost savings.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules and NSPE Code make the safety, health, and welfare of the public the engineer's paramount duty, which outranks a client's cost or schedule interests. Code-mandated safety factors exist to protect the public, so an engineer may not waive them at a client's request. Acting as a faithful agent never authorizes conduct that endangers the public.

front: During a confidential audit, an engineer discovers that a client's product has a defect posing a serious risk of injury to users. The client forbids any disclosure. What should the engineer do?
back: Protect the public: urge the client to correct and disclose the hazard, and if the client refuses, notify the appropriate authority. Public safety overrides confidentiality.
explanation: Engineers must normally keep client information confidential, but the Model Rules make public safety paramount and permit disclosure when needed to protect the public from danger. The confidentiality obligation yields when withholding information would endanger public health or safety. The engineer should first press the client to act, then notify the proper authority if the hazard persists.

front: An engineer recommending equipment to a client owns a significant financial stake in one of the vendors being considered. What does professional ethics require?
back: Fully and promptly disclose the financial interest to the client, and let the client decide (typically recusing from the selection). Undisclosed conflicts are prohibited.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules require engineers to disclose all known or potential conflicts of interest that could influence, or appear to influence, their judgment or the quality of their services. As faithful agents, engineers must place the client's interests first, so a personal financial stake in a candidate vendor must be disclosed openly. Concealing such an interest would compromise the engineer's objectivity and the client's trust.

front: A contractor bidding on a project that an engineer is administering offers the engineer expensive gifts and an all-expenses-paid vacation. How should the engineer respond?
back: Decline the gifts. Engineers must not accept valuable gratuities from parties dealing with their client or employer in connection with the engineer's work.
explanation: The Model Rules prohibit engineers from soliciting or accepting valuable gifts or gratuities, directly or indirectly, from contractors or others dealing with their client or employer on work for which the engineer is responsible. Accepting such gifts creates a conflict of interest and undermines the engineer's duty to act as a faithful, impartial agent. Preserving public trust and fair dealing requires declining.

front: May an engineer accept compensation from both the project owner and the equipment supplier for services on the same project?
back: Only if the circumstances are fully disclosed to and agreed upon by all parties; otherwise accepting compensation from more than one party for the same work is prohibited.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules bar engineers from accepting financial or other compensation from more than one party for services on the same project unless fully disclosed to and agreed upon by all interested parties. Undisclosed dual compensation is a conflict of interest that creates divided loyalties and compromises the engineer's role as a faithful agent. Transparency and consent are mandatory.

front: A licensed engineer is offered a fee to apply her professional seal to a set of drawings prepared entirely by an outside firm, which she did not prepare, supervise, or review. Is this acceptable?
back: No. An engineer may seal only work she prepared or that was produced under her responsible charge; sealing an outside party's unreviewed work ('plan stamping') is prohibited.
explanation: Under the NCEES Model Rules, a licensee may sign or seal only documents prepared by the licensee or under the licensee's responsible charge, meaning direct control and personal supervision. Stamping another party's work she did not supervise misrepresents responsibility and endangers the public, who rely on the seal as assurance of competent oversight. She must decline.

front: An engineer publishes a technical paper using substantial analysis and figures developed by a colleague, presenting the work as entirely her own. Which ethical obligation does this violate?
back: The duty to give credit for engineering work to those to whom it is due and to recognize others' contributions; taking a colleague's work as one's own is prohibited.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules require engineers to give credit for engineering work to those to whom credit is due and to recognize the proprietary interests of others. Presenting a colleague's analysis as one's own is a form of plagiarism that misrepresents authorship and is dishonest. Truthfulness and fair treatment of fellow professionals demand proper attribution.

front: A civil engineer with no background in high-voltage power systems is asked to independently design and certify a facility's medium-voltage electrical distribution. What is the ethical course of action?
back: Limit her role to her area of competence and associate a qualified electrical engineer for the rest (or decline). Engineers must perform services only where qualified by education or experience.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules require engineers to undertake assignments only when qualified in the specific technical field by education or experience. An engineer may take on a project outside her expertise only if she restricts her work to phases she is competent in while qualified associates handle and seal the remainder. Practicing beyond one's competence on safety-critical systems endangers the public.

front: A licensed engineer is asked to let an unlicensed individual use the engineer's seal so that person can offer engineering services to the public. Is this permissible?
back: No. Engineers must not aid or abet the unlicensed practice of engineering, and must not permit others to use their seal.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules prohibit licensees from aiding or abetting any person in the unlawful, unlicensed practice of engineering. Allowing an unlicensed person to use one's seal deceives the public about who is responsible for the work and circumvents licensure safeguards meant to protect public safety. The engineer must refuse.

front: An engineer is asked to issue a public statement, paid for by an advocacy group, praising a project's safety without revealing that the group funded and has an interest in the statement. What do the rules require?
back: The engineer must be objective and truthful and must disclose the identity and interest of the party on whose behalf he is speaking.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules require engineers to issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner and to reveal any interest the sponsoring party has in the matter. Undisclosed paid advocacy misleads the public and compromises the engineer's integrity. Honesty and transparency in public communications protect public welfare.

front: Serving as an expert witness, an engineer is asked by the retaining attorney to omit test results that weaken the client's position. How should the engineer proceed?
back: Refuse. Engineering reports, statements, and testimony must be objective and truthful and must include all relevant and pertinent information.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules require that engineers' professional reports, statements, and testimony be objective and truthful and contain all relevant and pertinent information. Selectively omitting unfavorable data would mislead the tribunal and violate the duty of honesty. The engineer's integrity obligation does not yield to a client's or attorney's litigation goals.

front: A client quietly hires an engineer to review and critique the work of another engineer who is still actively engaged by that same client on the ongoing project. What should the reviewing engineer do first?
back: Notify the other engineer before proceeding (unless that engineer's connection with the work has been terminated). Reviewing a peer's active work for the same client without their knowledge is improper.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules provide that an engineer shall not review the work of another engineer for the same client except with that engineer's knowledge, unless the reviewed engineer's connection with the work has ended. This preserves professional courtesy and protects reputations among licensees. The engineer should inform the other engineer before beginning the review.

front: To win a contract, a firm's engineer is tempted to overstate the firm's prior experience and list senior personnel who will not actually work on the project. Is this ethical?
back: No. Engineers must not misrepresent or exaggerate their own or the firm's qualifications, experience, or the personnel actually assigned to a project.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules require truthfulness and prohibit misrepresenting qualifications, experience, or responsibility for prior work. Padding a proposal with false experience or a personnel 'bait-and-switch' deceives the client and unfairly injures honest competitors. Integrity in soliciting and obtaining work is a core professional obligation.

front: An engineer becomes aware that another licensee has committed a violation of the rules of professional conduct that endangers the public. What do the Model Rules direct the engineer to do?
back: Report the information to the state licensing board and cooperate as requested; licensees aware of possible violations must provide information and assistance to the board.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules state that licensees having knowledge of possible violations shall provide the board with the information and assistance it requires. Reporting conduct that endangers the public upholds the paramount duty to protect public health, safety, and welfare. Such self-policing preserves the integrity and trustworthiness of the profession.

front: To be awarded a public contract, an engineering firm is asked to pay a 'finder's fee' to a public official's associate, contingent on the firm winning the award. May the firm agree?
back: No. Engineers must not offer or give, directly or indirectly, any gift, commission, or payment to secure work or influence the award of a contract by a public authority.
explanation: The NCEES Model Rules prohibit engineers from offering, giving, soliciting, or receiving, directly or indirectly, any commission, gift, or valuable consideration to secure work or influence a public contract award, apart from a bona fide fee to a legitimate employment or marketing agency. A contingent payment to influence an award is corruption and is unethical and likely unlawful. Fair competition and public trust forbid it.

front: A continuous-time LTI system produces output \(y_1(t)\) for input \(x_1(t)\) and \(y_2(t)\) for input \(x_2(t)\). Given \(y_1(t)=e^{-t}u(t)\) and \(y_2(t)=\cos(2t)\,u(t)\), find the output when the input is \(3x_1(t)-2x_2(t)\).
explanation: 1. LTI systems obey linearity, i.e. both scaling (homogeneity) and additivity. 2. A scaled sum of inputs therefore produces the same scaled sum of the corresponding outputs. 3. Hence \(3x_1-2x_2\) gives \(3y_1-2y_2=3e^{-t}u(t)-2\cos(2t)\,u(t)\).

front: Determine whether the system \(y(t)=t\,x(t)\) is time-invariant.
explanation: 1. Delay the input: feeding \(x(t-t_0)\) gives the response \(t\,x(t-t_0)\). 2. Delay the output: \(y(t-t_0)=(t-t_0)\,x(t-t_0)\). 3. Since \(t\,x(t-t_0)\neq (t-t_0)\,x(t-t_0)\), the two are unequal, so the explicit factor \(t\) makes the system time-varying.

front: Is the system \(y(t)=x^{2}(t)\) linear?
explanation: 1. Test homogeneity: scaling the input by \(a\) should scale the output by \(a\). 2. Input \(a\,x(t)\) gives \((a\,x(t))^{2}=a^{2}x^{2}(t)\). 3. Since \(a^{2}x^{2}(t)\neq a\,x^{2}(t)\) for general \(a\), homogeneity fails and the system is nonlinear.

front: A continuous-time LTI system has impulse response \(h(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)\). Find its unit-step response \(s(t)\).
explanation: 1. The step response is the running integral of the impulse response: \(s(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(\tau)\,d\tau\). 2. For \(t\ge 0\), \(s(t)=\int_{0}^{t}e^{-4\tau}\,d\tau=\left[-\tfrac14 e^{-4\tau}\right]_{0}^{t}\). 3. Evaluating gives \(s(t)=\tfrac14\left(1-e^{-4t}\right)\) for \(t\ge 0\).

front: The unit-step response of an LTI system is \(s(t)=(1-e^{-3t})u(t)\). Find the impulse response \(h(t)\).
explanation: 1. The impulse response is the derivative of the step response: \(h(t)=\dfrac{d}{dt}s(t)\). 2. Differentiating, the product-rule term \((1-e^{-3t})\delta(t)\) vanishes because \(1-e^{0}=0\). 3. The surviving term is \(h(t)=3e^{-3t}u(t)\).

front: A system with impulse response \(h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)\) is driven by \(x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)\). Find the output \(y(t)=x(t)*h(t)\).
explanation: 1. For \(t\ge 0\), \(y(t)=\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\tau}e^{-2(t-\tau)}\,d\tau\). 2. Factor out \(e^{-2t}\): \(y(t)=e^{-2t}\int_{0}^{t}e^{\tau}\,d\tau=e^{-2t}(e^{t}-1)\). 3. Simplify: \(y(t)=(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})u(t)\) (equivalently, invert \(\tfrac{1}{s+1}\cdot\tfrac{1}{s+2}\)).

front: Evaluate the convolution \(x(t)*\delta(t-3)\), where \(\delta(t)\) is the unit impulse.
explanation: 1. Convolution with the unit impulse reproduces the signal: \(x(t)*\delta(t)=x(t)\). 2. A time-shifted impulse shifts the signal by the same amount: \(x(t)*\delta(t-t_0)=x(t-t_0)\). 3. With \(t_0=3\), the result is \(x(t-3)\).

front: A system obeys \(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}}+7\dfrac{dy}{dt}+12\,y(t)=5\,x(t)\) with zero initial conditions. Find the transfer function \(H(s)=Y(s)/X(s)\).
explanation: 1. Laplace-transform each term with zero initial conditions: \(s^{2}Y+7sY+12Y=5X\). 2. Factor the left side: \((s^{2}+7s+12)Y(s)=5X(s)\). 3. Solve for the ratio: \(H(s)=\dfrac{5}{s^{2}+7s+12}=\dfrac{5}{(s+3)(s+4)}\).

front: A causal LTI system has \(H(s)=\dfrac{s+4}{s^{2}+2s+10}\). Find its zero and poles, and state whether it is BIBO stable.
back: Zero at \(s=-4\); poles at \(s=-1\pm 3j\); BIBO stable.
explanation: 1. Zero: set numerator \(s+4=0\Rightarrow s=-4\). 2. Poles: \(s^{2}+2s+10=0\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-40}}{2}=-1\pm 3j\). 3. Both poles have negative real part (\(-1\)), so they lie in the open left half-plane and the causal system is BIBO stable.

front: A causal LTI system has \(H(s)=\dfrac{10}{(s-2)(s+5)}\). Is it BIBO stable?
back: No - it is unstable (a pole at \(s=+2\) lies in the right half-plane).
explanation: 1. A causal system is BIBO stable only if every pole has a negative real part. 2. The poles are \(s=2\) and \(s=-5\). 3. Because \(s=2\) lies in the right half-plane, the system is not BIBO stable.

front: Find the DC gain of the stable LTI system \(H(s)=\dfrac{20}{s^{2}+6s+40}\).
explanation: 1. The DC gain is the steady-state response to a constant input, equal to \(H(s)\) evaluated at \(s=0\). 2. \(H(0)=\dfrac{20}{0+0+40}=\dfrac{20}{40}\). 3. DC gain \(=0.5\).

front: For \(H(s)=\dfrac{1}{s+10}\), find the magnitude and phase of the frequency response at \(\omega=10\ \text{rad/s}\).
